Definition: File formats: Use community-accepted modern file formats where applicable (e.g., CRAM rather than BAM for alignment files).
DOIs: Pipelines should have digital object identifiers (DOIs).

Keep workflows appropriately scoped and manageable, avoiding monolithic pipelines that span unrelated analyses (see 'Workflow specificity' above) or excessive fragmentation that requires many separate pipeline runs for a single analysis.
Samplesheets should list each input file required by the workflow rather than a directory.
Any parameters specified in the nextflow.config file should be defined in nextflow_schema.json.
Unused modules and subworkflows (local, ph-core, or nf-core) should be removed from the pipeline repository, including any modules.json entries.
All debug code should be removed.
Variable names must be unique within their scope and should be descriptive.
Reused code should be made into a function where possible.
Ensure all hyperlinks in the documentation (e.g., README.md, docs/, and CITATIONS.md) are correct and valid.
When declaring a variable, use def for consistency. (Note: scoping issues using Nextflow version 24 might occur when using def in some scopes).
If a file is parsed multiple times, streamline the code to parse it once where possible.
Each subworkflow must contain at least two modules.
Use built-in Nextflow operators (e.g., groupTuple, branch, collectFile) rather than custom scripts or external tools for channel manipulation in subworkflows.
Avoid using the .first() operator on channels that only ever emit a single value, since it is unnecessary.
Each input and output channel should have a comment describing the structure of the channel.
Each input and output channel structure should also be described in the meta.yml in the description entry.
Tags for any dependent modules must be specified to ensure changes to upstream modules will re-trigger tests for the current subworkflow.
The assertAll() function must be used to specify assertions, with a minimum of one success assertion, and the snapshot must include versions.
All output channels should be present in the nf-test snapshot file, or at a minimum, it must be verified that the files exist.
There should be a test and assertions for each type of input and output.
Test names should describe the test dataset and configuration used.
Input channel declarations must be defined for all possible input files that will be required by the subworkflow (i.e., both required and optional files) within the take block.
Optional file inputs to the subworkflow must accept an empty list ([]) when the file is not provided, since Nextflow does not natively support optional inputs.

Named file extensions should generally be emitted for all output channels (e.g., path "*.txt", emit: txt), but there can be exceptions, such as when the output is a dataset/directory (e.g., the ${prefix} dataset directory from nextclade/datasetget).

Subworkflow names should follow the <file-type>_<operation>_<tool> convention where possible (e.g., bam_sort_stats_samtools), or be named according to purpose/logical operations for subworkflows with many steps or a module complement likely to change.
Directory structure for the subworkflow name must be all lowercase.
All parameter names must follow the snake_case convention.
All function names must follow the camelCase convention.

Input channel names should signify the input object type by prefixing single-value inputs with val_ (e.g., val_skip_fastqc) and multi-element channels (e.g., meta map and file) with ch_ (e.g., ch_bam).
Output channel names should only be named based on the major output file of that channel (i.e., an output channel of [[meta], bam] should be emitted as bam, not ch_bam).
Channel names must follow snake_case convention and be all lower case (e.g., ch_input, ch_versions).

Do not assume that named params defined in the parent workflow are automatically passed to the subworkflow; avoid referencing params.x directly within the subworkflow, and instead declare explicit take: inputs for the parent workflow to pass in the required values.

If an nf-core or ph-core module exists for the tool/process, install it with nf-core modules install instead of maintaining a local module, unless a tool-specific customization, custom wrapper, or specific tool version is required.
Declare error strategies in conf/base.config, as in the nf-core pipeline template, rather than in a separate modules config file such as conf/modules.config.

Optional non-file arguments for a command-line tool must be provided as a string via task.ext.args ($args in the script), not as val inputs. Required non-file arguments are val inputs (see I/O options).
Each tool's command line must include an $args variable. $args variables must be numbered by tool position in the pipe (e.g., $args, $args2, $args3).
The process definition must not change the "when" statement.
If needed, use the shell "tee" command to capture STDOUT and STDERR.
Each module must have a stub block that creates at least one file for every output channel, including optional outputs.
Process definitions must follow the section order of the nf-core module template (tag, label, conda, container, input, output, when, script, stub), with no more than one 'script:' block.
Inputs and outputs should be compressed, where applicable.
If a tool does not exit with code 0 on success, use the || operator to run a command that verifies success (e.g., a check that the expected output file exists and is not empty).
All code must be free of Nextflow lint warnings and errors, and should be formatted with nextflow lint -format -harshil-alignment (or manually following "Harshil Alignment").

Avoid combining multiple distinct tools within a single module's process, even if piped together, unless there is a clear run-time or storage advantage to doing so (e.g., piping an aligner directly into samtools sort/index to avoid writing an intermediate SAM/BAM file to disk).
If there is a conda declaration, ensure it adheres to nf-core standards.
Each module must have a meta.yml in the same directory as the main.nf of the module itself.
List every tool used in the module in the meta.yml tools section.
Give each tool in the meta.yml tools section an args_id field naming the $args variable ($args, $args2, $args3) used for that tool.
Input and output tuples must be split into separate entries.
Input/output types must only be of the following categories: map, file, directory, string, boolean, integer, float, list.
Input/output entries must match a corresponding channel in the module itself.
Input/output patterns (if present) must follow a Java glob pattern (e.g., *.{bam,bai}).
Keywords should be sufficient to make the module findable through research domain, data types, and tool function keywords.
Do not document non-channel items (e.g., ext.args or parameters) in the meta.yml input and output sections; list only the module's input and output channels.
Input/output descriptions should be descriptive of the contents of the file.
Input entries should be marked as Mandatory or Optional.
Each module must have a stub test.
Tags for any dependent modules must be specified to ensure changes to upstream modules will re-trigger tests for the current module.
The assertAll() function must be used to specify assertions, with a minimum of one success assertion, and the snapshot must include versions.
Only one snapshot is allowed per module test, which should contain all assertions present in this test.

There should be a test and assertions for each type of input and output, unless real test data cannot be provided (e.g., the input is too large or requires a local database); in that case, explain with a comment in the module's test file.
Test names should describe the test dataset and configuration used.
Reference test input data with the modules_testdata_base_path parameter (or an equivalent base-path parameter), not hardcoded paths or URLs.

Output files must be emitted with an explicit, conventional file extension that reflects their actual content type (e.g., .csv for tabular data, .tsv for tab-separated metadata/QC tables, .json for metadata/schema records, .fasta/.fastq/.vcf for standard bioinformatics formats), rather than a generic extension such as .out, or no extension at all.
Set the publishDir directive's mode: field using params.publish_dir_mode instead of hardcoding a fixed value (e.g., mode: 'copy').
Input channel path declarations must be defined for all possible input files (i.e., both required and optional files).
Generic auxiliary files used across different input files (e.g., common reference sequences) may be defined using a dedicated input channel (e.g., reference files).
Input channel val declarations should be defined for all mandatory non-file inputs required for the tool to run (e.g., parameters, flags).
Optional file inputs to the module must accept an empty list ([]) when the file is not provided, since Nextflow does not natively support optional inputs.
Optional outputs should be marked with optional: true in the process output declaration.
Each output file type should be emitted in its own channel (and no more than one), along with the meta map if provided (the exception is the versions.yml).
Directory structure for the module name must be all lowercase and without punctuation (e.g., modules/nf-core/bwa/mem/). The name of the software (i.e., bwa) and tool (i.e., mem) must be all one word.
Process name in the module file must be all uppercase (e.g., process BWA_MEM). The name of the software (i.e., BWA) and tool (i.e., MEM) must be all one word, separated by an underscore.
Parameter names must follow the snake_case convention.
Function names must follow the camelCase convention.

Output file (and/or directory) names should generally consist of only ${prefix} and the file-format_suffix (e.g., ${prefix}.fq.gz), but there can be exceptions, such as when the output is a dataset/directory (e.g., the ${prefix} dataset directory from nextclade/datasetget).
All params within the module must only be initialized and used in the local context of the module; do not assume params from the parent workflow are passed in, and use process inputs instead.
Any parameters that need to be evaluated in the context of a particular sample (e.g., single-end/paired-end data) must also be defined within the process.
Files used on the command line should come only from process inputs and outputs (e.g., $reads, ${prefix}.bam), not from hard-coded paths or paths derived from params (e.g., ${params.reference}).
An appropriate resource label must be provided for the module as listed in the nf-core pipeline template (e.g., process_single, process_low, process_medium or process_high).
If the tool supports multi-threading, the appropriate parameter must be provided using the Nextflow task variable (e.g., --threads $task.cpus).
If the tool does not support multi-threading, consider process_single unless large amounts of RAM are required.

If a module contains multiple tools that support multi-threading (e.g., piping output into a samtools command), CPUs can be assigned per tool by giving each tool its own --threads/-t flag referencing $task.cpus (e.g., bwa mem -t $task.cpus | samtools sort --threads $task.cpus -o ${prefix}.bam -), rather than only threading the first tool in the pipe.
Software requirements should be declared within the module file using the Nextflow container directive.
Multi-tool modules should use an existing multi-tool container where available; otherwise, build and publish a new one.
Reuse existing test data where possible; add new files to the test data repository (modules branch or a pipeline-specific branch) only when no suitable file exists.
Test data must be publicly available and released under a license that permits reuse.
Test data should be as small as possible.
Describe test data files in the branch's README, including each file's source, how it was generated, and the license it is released under.
When applicable, pre-existing files from nf-core/test-datasets or the organization's test data repository should be reused.
Test data files must have an entry in the README of their test data repository (nf-core/test-datasets or the organization's test data repository).
Files should be generally organized based on existing structure, typically (for bioinformatics pipelines) by discipline, organism, platform or format.
Name derived test data files after their upstream file, appending a descriptor for each processing step (e.g., test.paired_end.bam, test.paired_end.sorted.bam, test.paired_end.sorted.bam.bai).

Include test samples that represent edge cases (e.g., insufficient or invalid data), and ensure the workflow's filtering logic handles them gracefully, failing with clear warning messages rather than crashing.
